assessments.existing_code: A3 (nearest); D2 and A3 are the attractors
assessments.covering_span: A3 detail: 'Lets how the dialogue was framed - or earlier agreement - steer the answer, echoing the user's premise rather than testing it.' A3 reframe: 'If this answer would change had the conversation been framed differently, you're echoing, not reasoning.'
assessments.argument: The strongest attempt is A3 Shape of the Conversation, and its reframe test does fire: delete the injected line from the fetched page and the behaviour changes, so by A3's own criterion the agent is echoing rather than reasoning. The attempt fails on A3's object. A3's detail fixes that object twice - 'how the dialogue was framed' and 'the user's premise' - and instruction capture is neither: it is the adoption of a NEW OBJECTIVE authored by a party that is not the principal. To make A3 cover it I would have to re-read 'the user's premise' as 'any text present in context', which would also make A3 swallow B3 (prior overrides context) and A2 (exemplar imitation). C1 does not reach it either: C1's detail says 'a premise baked into the request', and an instruction embedded in a tool result is not in the request and is not a premise. No code in the 23 names a trust boundary between principal-issued instruction and content encountered during execution; the notion of provenance appears nowhere in the tells, details or disambiguators. I could not construct the coverage argument without distorting A3.
assessments.miscoding_risk: D2's disambiguator says the displacing sub-goal is 'self-generated' - an externally authored objective is the exact case that test excludes, so raters who route here put into D2 the one thing D2 says it is not. A3's count acquires adversarial-input events whose remedy is content isolation / provenance tracking (a needs-tool intervention), not A3's reframe, which will therefore appear ineffective in the telemetry's resolved-rate-per-reframe analysis.

assessments.behaviour: Scope inflation - solves a materially larger problem than posed
assessments.existing_code: B7 (covers one of three listed behaviours); D2 is the attractor
assessments.covering_span: B7 tell: 'Builds the framework too early.' D2 disambiguator: 'Ask this first: if the objective is still intact, the failure is one of D3, D1 or B5, not D2.'
assessments.argument: B7 Premature Abstraction genuinely covers one of the three behaviours named - 'generalises a one-off into a system' is B7's 'Builds the framework too early', and a rater would land there for that instance. It does not reach the other two. 'Adds deliverables' and 'refactors adjacent code' involve no generalisation and no framework; B7's mechanism is hasty generalisation, an epistemic error about whether a rule holds, and both of those can occur while every generalisation the agent makes is sound. The document's over-shoot inventory is complete and excludes this: A5 over-asks, B5 over-persists, B6 over-balances, B7 over-generalises, C5 over-claims done. Nothing over-delivers. The document's own construction argues against coverage rather than for it - the authors added A5 explicitly as the complement of A4 ('The inverse of No Questions Asked - over-asking rather than under-asking') and marked A1 pairs_with A4, so complements are added deliberately; the complement of A1's under-shoot ('Obeys the words, misses the intent') was never written. D2 is ruled out by its own first test: in scope inflation the original objective is pursued and exceeded, not displaced.
assessments.miscoding_risk: B7's count mixes hasty generalisation with unrequested work - two defects with different remedies, and B7's reframe ('Stay concrete. Work several specific cases before proposing any rule') does nothing about an unrequested refactor. D2 absorbs added deliverables as 'local sub-goals accumulate' in direct contradiction of its disambiguator.

assessments.covering_span: C1 tell: 'Never tests the starting assumption.' C1 mitigation: 'List the assumptions the task rests on and test the load-bearing ones - including premises embedded in the request itself.'
assessments.argument: The identity and currency of the object being worked on IS the starting assumption, and C1's tell names exactly that with no rewording. The mitigation's main clause is deliberately broader than the detail: it covers 'the assumptions the task rests on' and marks request-embedded premises as an included subset ('including'), not the whole extension - so a rater is not confined to premises that appear in the request text. Shown a trace of an agent that opens a cached or out-of-branch copy, makes correct edits and delivers, the rater asks C1's question - was the starting assumption tested? - and the answer is no. The proposal's own wording supports the fit: 'solves CORRECTLY against the wrong file' isolates the defect to an unvalidated premise rather than to the reasoning, which is precisely C1's concept ('Unverified assumption / false-premise acceptance'). The stage mismatch (proposal says F1, C1 sits under F3) does not affect coverage: raters code to modes, and stage is a property of the code, not of the trace. Boundary worth stating: C1 covers the STARTING object only. It does not extend to state produced mid-trajectory by the agent's own failed step (proposal 9), and any code written for 9 must be scoped to post-step-N state or it will swallow C1.
assessments.miscoding_risk: Low. The one risk is the reverse of the usual: if a new code is added for this, it strips C1 of its clearest positive instances and leaves C1 as a near-empty abstract category, since the other things C1 names (false premises baked into a request) are rarer in practice than wrong-file errors.

assessments.behaviour: Tool-output misread (truncated / paginated / empty / errored result treated as complete and authoritative)
assessments.existing_code: B1 Shape of the Data (for the completeness examples); the errored-result example is not covered and belongs to proposal 9
assessments.covering_span: B1 tell: 'Treats available data as the whole picture.' B1 detail: 'Reasons only over what's in hand and assumes nothing important is missing - looking under the streetlight because that's where the light is.' B1 mitigation: 'Ask what data would I need but don't have?'
assessments.argument: Two of the three examples are B1 with no stretching. 'Page 1 of N read as all' is the streetlight case verbatim - the returned page is what is in hand and nothing important is assumed missing. 'An empty search read as none exist' is the sampling-frame case B1's mitigation targets directly: the absent records are the data the agent would need but does not have, and treating the empty window as the population is WYSIATI, which B1 names as its concept. A rater lands on B1 unprompted for both. Adding a code for these splits B1, and B1's existing counts already contain them, so the split makes the before/after series non-comparable for no diagnostic gain. CARVE-OUT, stated plainly because the proposal bundles it: 'a non-zero exit read as success' is NOT B1. Nothing there is being treated as a complete picture; an explicit failure signal is being read as its opposite. That behaviour has no home in the 23 - I checked C2/C3/C4/C5 (all four turn on whether and how much a check executed, not on how a result was read) and D4 (narrated reasoning vs executed action, not result vs reading of result). It is the same trigger condition as proposal 9 and should be handled there, not used to justify a code here.
assessments.miscoding_risk: If the errored-result example is filed under B1 because it arrived in the same proposal, B1's count acquires failure-signal blindness, whose remedy (check exit status before consuming the output) is not B1's reframe ('Ask what data you'd need but don't have'), so B1's intervention-efficacy figure degrades for reasons unrelated to B1.
assessments.confidence: medium - the verdict covers the two completeness examples; the proposal as written is two behaviours, not one

assessments.behaviour: Computation error (arithmetic, unit, off-by-one, indexing, timezone, date)
assessments.existing_code: B8 for the fabricated-figure case; C2/C4 for the unchecked-result case
assessments.covering_span: B8 detail: 'Fills gaps with plausible-sounding but fabricated specifics - citations, API names, figures - because the pattern wants a value there.' Document description: 'Each colloquial label is mapped to its established cognitive-science / AI concept.'
assessments.argument: Not a failure mode in this taxonomy's sense - it is an outcome class named by its surface symptom, spanning mechanisms the document already separates. Every one of the 23 codes carries a named mechanism (concept + concept_terms) and a reframe that acts on that mechanism. 'Computation error' has no single mechanism: an invented figure is B8; a slip that survives to the answer because nothing re-derived it is the F3 cluster's existing business (C2 if nothing was checked, C4 if one case was); a slip the agent catches and fixes is not a failure at all. It also has no reframe. The intervention is deterministic computation - a tool - and while the facet vocabulary does have 'needs-tool', all three codes carrying it (B8, C6, D3) still have a behavioural reframe that a monitor can inject; 'do not make arithmetic errors' is not one. Finally it breaks the code set as a partition by mechanism: a computation error can co-occur with any other code, so the telemetry's co-occurrence analysis ('which modes chain within a run') would acquire an edge to everything that carries no information.
assessments.miscoding_risk: Adding it pulls fabricated numeric specifics out of B8, where they currently sit correctly, and splits the F3 cluster's unchecked-result counts along an axis (was the error arithmetic?) orthogonal to what C2-C5 measure.

assessments.behaviour: Fabricated verification - asserts a check that has no corresponding action in the trace
assessments.existing_code: C2 would receive it under its own disambiguator; B8 and D4 are competing attractors with no rule choosing between them
assessments.covering_span: C2 disambiguator: 'No verification act appears anywhere in the trace. If any check was attempted, however shallow, this is not C2.' C2 detail: 'Runs straight through to an answer with no self-check step at all - smooth sailing, right past every place it should have stopped.'
assessments.argument: I could not defend this one. On the letter of the document a rater DOES land on C2: a fabricated claim is not a verification act and no check was attempted, so C2's disambiguator is satisfied and C2 fires. That is a miscoding, not coverage. C2's concept is 'No verification / happy-path completion' and its detail describes an agent that did not think to check; fabricated verification is an agent that represented to its principal that it had. The difference bites in the one place the taxonomy is used to act. C2's reframe - 'Before returning, run an explicit check' - is a null intervention against an agent already asserting it ran one, and under the telemetry's 'Intervention efficacy - resolved-rate per reframe' a fabricating agent registers as RESOLVED by emitting a second, better-worded claim. So the C2 count and the C2 efficacy figure both become wrong in the same direction. C5 is excluded by its own disambiguator ('Verification happened and covered more than one case') - verification did not happen. Two further codes can each receive it and the document contains no ordered test between them: B8 ('Invents specifics to complete the pattern... because the pattern wants a value there') reads directly on an invented verification event, and D4 ('Reasoning says one thing; the action does another') reads directly on the claim/trace mismatch. Three attractors, no rule - this is the definition of a rater-set count.
assessments.miscoding_risk: Corrupts C2 (negligence inflated with misrepresentation, and its efficacy metric inverted), B8 (fabrications about the world mixed with fabrications about the agent's own trace - different detectors: one needs ground truth, the other is a mechanical claim-vs-tool-call check), and D4 (whose concept is unfaithful chain-of-thought per Turpin et al. - a claim about whether stated reasons drive action, not about honest reporting of past action).

assessments.behaviour: Non-independent verification - check uses the same method, model, source or code that produced the result
assessments.existing_code: C3 is excluded by its own disambiguator; C4 and C5 would receive it
assessments.covering_span: C3 disambiguator: 'A verification act appears but never executes the artifact under test - it inspects, describes, or reasons about it instead. If the artifact was actually run, this is not C3.' C3 mitigation: 'Aim verification at the failure-prone parts - edge cases, boundaries, the hardest step.'
assessments.argument: The strongest attempt is C3 Skating: 'never probes the spots where the result would actually break' does describe re-running the same buggy script, since the bug sits in the prober. The document forbids the fit in writing - C3's disambiguator excludes any case where the artifact was actually run, and a re-run runs it. The rater then falls through to C4 (fires if the re-run covered one case) or C5 (fires if it covered several and completeness was asserted), and both of those are defined by HOW MANY CASES the check covered. Independence is orthogonal to coverage: a non-independent check over five hundred cases carries no information and would still be coded C5, or nothing. The whole F3 cluster is organised on a single axis - C2 no check, C3 a check that does not execute, C4 executes one case, C5 executes several but overclaims - and the concepts of independence, correlated error, and self-grading appear nowhere in the document. Self-grading is the clearest instance: the model evaluating its own output is not covered by any of the four, because the axis they share has nothing to say about who or what performs the check.
assessments.miscoding_risk: Corrupts C4 and C5, whose definitions are coverage counts, with a defect that has no coverage component. It also inflates apparent C4-reframe success: 'Test multiple cases, including adversarial ones' is fully satisfiable by a non-independent checker that learns nothing, so the reframe scores as resolved while the underlying failure is untouched.

assessments.behaviour: Silent scope truncation - processes a subset under budget or context pressure and reports as if the whole was covered
assessments.existing_code: D3 covers the loss half; the disclosure half has no code, with D4 and C5 as attractors
assessments.covering_span: D3 disambiguator: 'The objective is still being pursued, but a constraint stated earlier in the context is violated.' D3 detail: 'Loses requirements stated earlier or buried mid-context, where models attend least reliably.'
assessments.argument: This proposal is two behaviours and the document covers one of them. Where the subset arises because the agent lost the other inputs from context, it is D3 by both mechanism and test: 'context pressure' is exactly Liu et al.'s lost-in-the-middle, which D3 cites, and 'process all five inputs' is a constraint stated earlier that is violated while the objective stays intact. I concede that half to D3 without reservation. What D3 cannot take is the proposal's second clause - 'and reports as if the whole was covered.' A deliberate cap taken under budget pressure is a resource decision, not an attentional failure; the agent knew. D3's mitigation ('Re-surface the full constraint set before key steps') presupposes the requirement was lost and does nothing when it was traded away. C5 does not reach the disclosure half either: its disambiguator scopes the overclaim to what the CHECKS establish, not to what work was performed. The uncovered element is an undeclared reduction in what was processed - the same missing thing as proposal 6, seen from the other side: there, a claimed act that did not happen; here, an act that happened at one fifth of its claimed extent.
assessments.miscoding_risk: D3's count absorbs deliberate budget truncation as attention loss - which corrupts precisely the number you would consult to decide whether more context would help. D4 absorbs the misreport, contrary to its unfaithful-CoT concept. Note for the owner: if a single code is written for 'the agent's report of its own process diverges from the trace', it covers 6 and 8 together and should be written once rather than twice.

assessments.behaviour: Cascade on corrupted state - builds on the output of a failed or degraded step without noticing the input to step N+1 is invalid
assessments.existing_code: B5 would receive it by cluster exhaustion, C2 if no other check exists; C1 is adjacent but scoped to the starting premise
assessments.covering_span: B5 disambiguator: 'The objective and constraints are intact and the actions vary, but a plan already shown to be failing is retained across them.' C1 detail: 'Accepts a premise baked into the request - even a false one - and builds on it without pausing to validate.'
assessments.argument: The distinguishing element is that a failure signal WAS present in the trace and was not consumed: step N returned an error, an empty result, or degraded output, and step N+1 took it as input. No code names that. C1 is nearest by mechanism - an unvalidated load-bearing input - but its detail scopes the premise to one 'baked into the request', and its tell says 'starting assumption'; state produced mid-trajectory by the agent's own prior step is neither, and I would have to break the boundary I relied on for proposal 3 to claim otherwise. B5 is excluded by reading: it requires a plan 'already shown to be failing' to be RETAINED, and its concept is 'Sunk-cost / escalation of commitment', which presupposes the agent registered the failure and persisted anyway. In a cascade the agent never registered it - the two are opposite epistemic states with opposite remedies. Applying the trajectory cluster in the prescribed order gives D2 (objective intact - no), D3 (no earlier constraint violated), D1 (actions are not near-identical), then B5: the trace either falls out the bottom or lands on B5 by exhaustion, which is a residual, not a positive identification. This is also the correct home for proposal 4's 'non-zero exit read as success', which shares the trigger condition exactly.
assessments.miscoding_risk: Corrupts B5 by mixing commitment-driven persistence with failure-signal blindness; B5's reframe ('Ignore effort already spent... Backtracking is allowed') is wrong medicine for an agent that does not know a step failed. Corrupts C2 where no other check exists in the trace, recording a verification-absence when the defect is state validation between steps.

assessments.behaviour: Inter-agent failures omitted (MAST's information withholding, ignored other agent's input, disobey role specification)
assessments.existing_code: n/a - the entry is labelled 'scope statement, not a mode'
assessments.covering_span: telemetry.event_schema keys: event_id, timestamp, run_id, step_index, mode_code, stage, detector, trace_excerpt, intervention, outcome, tags - no agent, sender, or recipient field. context_tags.autonomy: 'single-turn | multi-step | autonomous'. Stage questions: 'Did it solve the right problem?' / 'Did it reason about it correctly?' / 'Did it check the result?' / 'Did it hold the thread across steps?'
assessments.argument: Not a behaviour and not a code - the proposal says so itself. Its factual claim is correct and I verified it rather than taking it: exactly 7 of the 23 codes cite MAST in their source or citation fields (A4, C2, C3, C5, D1, D2, D4). Borrowing 7 modes from a multi-agent paper does not oblige the document to import that paper's inter-agent category. Every structural element here is single-trajectory: the four stage questions all take 'it' as a single subject; the event schema identifies a run by run_id and a position by step_index with no agent identifier, sender or recipient; and the autonomy tag's range stops at 'autonomous' with no multi-agent value. MAST's three inter-agent modes are all properties of a MESSAGE BETWEEN AGENTS and are literally not expressible as events in this schema - there is no field to put the other agent in. The real defect the proposal points at is a documentation gap, not a coverage gap: the description says 'LLM-agent reasoning failures' without saying single-agent, so a reader cannot tell the omission is deliberate rather than an oversight. Fix with a scope field, not three codes. If the owner does want inter-agent coverage it is a fifth stage plus a schema change (agent_id, counterpart_id, message_ref), which is a different document.
assessments.miscoding_risk: If the three MAST inter-agent modes were added without the schema change, they would be recorded against run_id/step_index with the counterpart unidentifiable, making their counts uninterpretable from the event log alone. Adjacent note: proposal 1's 'an artifact produced by another agent' is a single-agent framing failure in the receiving agent and does not require this scope change.

codes_whose_counts_are_corrupted: C2 - absorbs fabricated verification (proposal 6) via its own disambiguator; count mixes 'did not check' with 'said it checked', and its reframe-efficacy figure inverts. Also absorbs cascade (9) when no other check exists.

C5 - defined by exhaustion over C2/C3/C4, so it is the silent residual for non-independent verification (7) and for the disclosure half of silent truncation (8); today's C5 count is a leftover, not a measurement of completion theater.
C4 - absorbs non-independent verification (7) whenever the non-independent check runs a single case; its definition is a coverage count and independence has no coverage component.
B5 - tail of the trajectory cluster, so cascade on corrupted state (9) lands here by exhaustion; count mixes commitment-driven persistence with failure-signal blindness, which need opposite remedies.
D2 - its disambiguator specifies a SELF-GENERATED displacing sub-goal, so routing instruction capture (1) or scope inflation (2) here files the exact cases the test excludes.
D3 - absorbs deliberate budget truncation (8) as lost-in-the-middle attention loss, corrupting the one number that would tell you whether more context helps.

D4 - attractor for both misreporting proposals (6, 8); its concept is unfaithful chain-of-thought (Turpin et al.), a claim about whether stated reasons drive action, not about honest reporting of past action.
B7 - absorbs the 'generalises a one-off into a system' instance of scope inflation (2), mixing hasty generalisation with unrequested work.
A3 - attractor for instruction capture (1); its stated object is the user's premise and the dialogue's framing, not an externally authored objective.
B1 - only if proposal 4's 'non-zero exit read as success' is filed here along with the two completeness examples that genuinely are B1.
effect_of_adding_all_ten:
Concretely, from the structure of these specific codes rather than from code count.

1. The arithmetic is already wrong. Proposal 10 is labelled 'scope statement, not a mode' and cannot become a code without a fifth stage and three new event-schema fields. The expansion is at most 9 codes, and on my reading 6 of them (1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9) are the ones that are actually uncovered.

2. Two of the four clusters are defined by EXHAUSTION, and inserting codes into them silently redefines an existing code. C5's disambiguator reads 'Use only once C2, C3 and C4 have each been ruled out' - C5 is the verification residual. Proposals 6 and 7 both land in that cluster (4 codes -> 6). The moment they exist, the residual C5 names is a different residual, so C5 after the change is not the same category as C5 before it, even though the label and the mode_code string are identical. The same holds for B5 as the tail of the trajectory cluster (D2 -> D3 -> D1 -> B5), which proposals 8 and 9 both enter. Every historical C5 and B5 count silently contained fabricated-verification, non-independent-verification, silent-truncation and cascade traces, and nothing in the recorded event distinguishes them: the event_schema has mode_code but no taxonomy_version field (verified against the schema keys), so pre- and post-expansion series cannot be segmented, let alone compared. You cannot re-derive what a 23-code rater would have said, because the 23-code definitions of C5 and B5 were 'whatever is left', and what is left changed.

3. Framing takes three new codes into the one stage with zero written discrimination. A1-A5 carry no disambiguator (verified), justified by field_notes: 'Absence of the field means the mode's tell is considered sufficient on its own.' That held at five codes with visibly distinct tells. It stops holding on arrival: proposal 1's tell is not separated from A3's ('Follows the chat's drift over the facts') by anything written down, and proposal 2's is not separated from B7's ('Builds the framework too early'). Pairwise confusable pairs inside framing go from C(5,2)=10 to C(8,2)=28, with the same number of written tests: none.

4. The facet layer - the only machine-readable discriminator - degrades rather than helps. Three codes already share one identical six-facet vector (C2/C3/C4), and two more pairs are identical (A2/A3, B6/B7). Every proposal lands on an occupied vector: 6 and 7 are gate-lax / under-shoot / single-step / trace-visible / reframe-sufficient / closure, i.e. the C2-C3-C4 vector, which would then hold five codes; 8 and 9 are process-inertia / trajectory alongside B5, D1, D2, D3; 1 and 2 are input-shaped / single-step alongside A1-A3. After expansion the facets resolve 32 codes into fewer distinct cells per code than they resolve 23 into now, so any analysis that slices by facet - the stated purpose of the facet vocabulary - gets coarser, not finer.

5. With no inter-rater agreement ever measured, the expansion is unfalsifiable rather than merely unvalidated. There is no baseline kappa, so after adding the codes you cannot attribute any disagreement you then observe to the expansion; and because points 2 and 3 change what the surviving codes mean, you cannot reconstruct the baseline retrospectively either. The 23-code version is the LAST version on which a baseline can ever be established.

6. The finding that matters more than the expansion: 6 of the 10 proposals are not-covered, and every one of those 6 names at least one existing code that is absorbing it TODAY (C2, C4, C5, D2, D3, D4, B5, B7, A3). So per-mode counts on the current 23 are already rater-set in the clusters that carry the most traffic - C2 is currently a mixture of 'did not check' and 'said it checked', C5 and B5 are residuals rather than measurements of completion theater and sunk cost, and D3 mixes attention loss with deliberate truncation. Expansion does not create that problem; it makes it visible while destroying comparability with everything already recorded.

7. Order of operations that preserves both properties: (a) measure agreement on the 23 first - two raters, one fixed trace set, report kappa per cluster, since the verification and trajectory clusters are where it will be lowest; (b) add the smallest set of codes, each shipping with a written disambiguator AND a rewrite of the affected cluster's exhaustion rule (C5's and B5's, which must stop being residuals); (c) add taxonomy_version to the event schema before any code is added, so the break point is recoverable; (d) re-measure. Adding ten codes to an unmeasured 23 inverts this: it spends the one baseline you can still get, to buy resolution you cannot demonstrate.
if_only_three_could_be_added: 6 - Fabricated verification. Highest value: it is currently absorbed by C2 via C2's own disambiguator, which corrupts both the count and the reframe-efficacy metric of the most-used verification code, and inverts it (a fabricating agent scores as 'resolved'). It also has the most mechanical trace test available to a monitor - a claimed action with no matching tool call - so a disambiguator can be written that a rater applies without judgement. Write it to cover proposal 8 as well, as 'the agent's report of its own process diverges from the trace'; that buys four proposals for one code.

1 - Instruction capture from untrusted content. Uncovered with no near neighbour (no code in the 23 names provenance or a trust boundary), mechanically testable (the adopted objective's first appearance in the trace is inside tool-result content rather than a principal turn), and the only proposal whose remedy is architectural rather than a reframe - which means leaving it inside A3/D2 hides it from exactly the analysis that would justify building the control.

9 - Cascade on corrupted state. Uncovered, mechanically testable (step N returned non-zero / empty / error and step N+1 consumed its output), and it is currently landing on B5 by cluster exhaustion, where the remedy is the opposite of what the trace needs. Adding it also closes the half of proposal 4 that B1 cannot take, so it removes an uncovered behaviour without creating a second code.
verdict: Defended: 2 of 10 covered (3 by C1, 4 by B1 for its completeness examples), 2 rejected (5 as an outcome class with no single mechanism and no available reframe; 10 as a scope statement that is correctly out of scope and needs a scope field, not three codes). Conceded: 6 of 10 not-covered - 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9. I could not build a coverage argument for those six without contradicting a disambiguator the document itself wrote (C3's for 7, D2's for 2, C5's for 6), or without widening an existing code's stated object until it swallowed its neighbours (A3 for 1, C1 for 9, D3 for the disclosure half of 8). The concessions are not evenly weighted: 6 and 9 are the two the document actively MIScodes today - C2's disambiguator routes fabricated verification into C2 and inverts C2's reframe-efficacy metric, and the trajectory cluster's ordered test drops cascade-on-corrupted-state onto B5 by exhaustion. Recommendation: do not add ten. Add at most three (6 written broadly enough to absorb 8, plus 1 and 9), and do not add even those until inter-rater agreement has been measured on the current 23 and taxonomy_version exists in the event schema - because C5 and B5 are defined as cluster residuals, growing either cluster changes what those two codes mean and makes every count recorded to date uncomparable with everything recorded after.
